mission.target: Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο
mission.purpose: Νέα πραγματική αναζήτηση πηγών για ορμητήρια, αγκυροβόλια και καταφύγια πειρατών και κουρσάρων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο, 1600–1700. Αναζήτησε σε όλες τις έντεκα οικογένειες πηγών, περιηγητές, portolans, σύγχρονα κείμενα, αρχεία και μεταγενέστερες μελέτες. Απόκτησε τα προσβάσιμα πραγματικά κείμενα. Για κάθε εύρημα δώσε ιστορικό τοπωνύμιο, σύγχρονη ταύτιση και γεωγραφική θέση μόνο όπου τεκμηριώνονται, χρονολογία, χρήστες, είδος χρήσης, ακριβή πηγή, σελίδα ή φύλλο ή αρχειακή αναφορά, ακριβές απόσπασμα, confidence και verification status. Ξεχώρισε αναφορά πηγής, ερμηνεία και υπόθεση, μεταγενέστερη μελέτη από πρωτογενές τεκμήριο και ορμητήριο από τόπο επιδρομής. Μην μετατρέπεις τη χρονολογία του ερωτήματος σε χρονολογία αχρονολόγητου γεγονότος. Δήλωσε απρόσιτα αρχεία και ανεξέταστο υλικό. Καμία αυτόματη ιστορική επαλήθευση.

claims.title: Occasioned by the death of Creveliers off Astypalaia: The island's role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century

place.canonical_name: Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο

claims.acquired_text_excerpt:
Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis
Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted VenetianOttoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

historien, étudiant les données des sommes annuelles que les Vénitiens avaient
perçues finalement de chaque île des Cyclades entre 1684 et 1693, a constaté des
fluctuations dans les sommes, mais aussi des interruptions dans le versement des
taxes. Il a considéré qu’elles étaient dues à l’inefficacité des percepteurs d’impôt

Captain Spratt in the 1860s describes the presence of guard posts or look-outs “upon the most conspicuous
eminences along the whole coast of Crete, at distances of eight or ten miles apart, whose beacon-fires blaze up at
dusk, if a vessel comes in sight, in order to warn the neighbouring villages authorities that a strange sail is off the
coast. It is doubtless a custom handed down from the earliest times, especially when piracy was frequent” (Spratt
1865, 3). A similar system was recently described by Andrew Blackler (2022) and a series of soroi, beacons or
pyres, have been identified in the Pediada of Crete. These could have been used for signaling and alerting in case
of attacks (Sarris et al. 2011; Panagiotaki et al. 2020). Steven Soetens (2005, 44) too has noted the similarities
between the various lookouts as shown on a Venetian map (Fig. 4) drawn by Nicola Gualdo de Priorati in 1633
and the location of peak sanctuaries (Arakadaki 1997). Could these, besides their ritual functions, also have
represented an early warning system, protecting the Cretan coasts during the heydays of Minoan civilization?
A combination of evenly spaced coastal settlements, peak sanctuaries with large vistas and beacons that could
be used in a way that tradition suggests the fall of Troy was announced would have represented a considerable
“AWACS”.
And then there is the question of pirate attacks of coastal settlements – as I said they don’t leave their
­signature and thus it is difficult to blame pirates rather than another adversary for the destruction and pillaging
of a settlement. A much-cited example is the Late Cycladic (LC) IIIC site of Koukounaries on Paros. Because
of the discovery of bodies within the destruction layer, its excavator, Dimitrios Schilardi (1979; 1984), blamed
pirates, but apparently the site was not pillaged, which would be strange in case of a pirate attack (Vlachopoulos
2003). Each site in fact should be explored in detail: How did the destruction happen? Was it partial or ­complete?
Pirates would, I think, rarely destroy a site entirely since it would be to their benefit if the settlement r­ ecovered
so that it could be pillaged again. Bergen in Norway, for example, was pillaged by pirates in 1428, 1429 and 1432
and although partly burned, enough was left to allow recovery (Stylegar et al. 2020).
If a site was pillaged, can we identify its objects elsewhere? Or objects from one culture in another area,
without these being the result of trade? Or is there a concentration of unexplained wealth in modest coastal
settlements, like, for example, at Mochlos or even Petras? Such finds do not necessarily imply that these sites
themselves were pirate nests, but they may have provided safe havens for pirates to stock up and exchange valuables for foodstuffs.

problem. Was this the result of internal strife, an attack by a Mainland competitor, or could it have been raided

these authors report that Julius Caesar was apprehended near Pharmakoussa. The only exception is Polyaenus,
according to whom the pirates captured their famous victim close to Cape Maleas in the Peloponnese and
­remained outside the walls of Miletus until the ransom was delivered. This reference implicitly suggests that
Pharmakoussa ­belonged to the chora of Miletus.
Plutarch and Polyaenus refer to the pirates who captured Julius Caesar as Cilicians, while the other sources
do not specify their identity. Therefore, it cannot be certain whether the pirates were Cilicians, Milesians or
whether a mixed band − a fairly common occurrence in pirate crews. Perhaps, there was confusion between
the terms Cilicians and pirates (App. Mith. 14.92) or perhaps the pirates presented themselves as coming from
a distant homeland (e.g., Cilicia), to hide their real identity and to protect (nearby) homeland from reprisals, or perhaps the relevant sources, which are all considerably later than the event, wanted to attribute the
incident to some unknown or foreign pirates. Indeed, after the final defeat of Mithridates and the end of the
­Mithridatic wars, cities like Miletus ceased trying to strike a balance between the two conflicting powers (Rome
and ­Mithridates) and sided, willingly or unwillingly, with Rome (see Kleiner 1968, 19; Sarantidis 2020, 55−6;
Cicero (Verr. 2.1.89), likewise, refers to the imposition of taxes “by the Roman people” and the participation of
Miletus in the expulsion of the pirates).
In any event, whether the pirates had Pharmakoussa as their base or were operating outside of it, or
whether they happened to locate themselves in the vicinity only once, it is difficult to accept the idea that they
went ­unnoticed by a passing ship or by guard troops, given the presence of defensive forts and watchtowers
throughout the Milesian seaboard territories, including those on Pharmakoussa itself (for the supervision of
these islands, see Sarantidis 2020, 203–23, figs. 112–21). Moreover, both the undisturbed visit of a large group of
men anchored in an island cove for thirty-eight days, and the fact that Julius Caesar himself, after he redeemed
himself and assembled a fleet, returned to the island to find the pirates still situated at the same place, would
seem to indicate that the pirates in question were able to reside on these islands (or, at least, on Pharmakoussa)
and conduct their activities unhindered during this period.
However, pirate activity in this islandscape was not limited to antiquity; in fact, pirates continued to operate
there in modern times. The Englishman Anthony Roberts, a pirate who was himself taken hostage by pirates in
1692, describes the seasonal but systematic use of the region by pirates, stating that after wintering on islands,
such as Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Melos, pirates would sail to Phournoi in early March: “And then they go for the
Furnoes [Phournoi], and lie there under the high land hid, having a watch on the hill with a little flag, whereby
they make a signal, if they see any sail; they flip out, and lie athwart the boak of Samos, and take their prize;
they lie in the same nature under Necaria [Ikaria], and Gadronise [Gaidouronisi], and Leppiso [Leipsoi] in
the spring and forepart of the summer” (Hacke 1699, 8; see also Koutsouflakis, this volume; Koutzakiotis, this
volume). It should be noted that Gaidouronisi is an earlier name for Agathonisi, which continued to be used as
a pirate site in the following century (see Krantonelli 1998, 110, 179).

SURVEY EVIDENCE IN WESTERN ROUGH CILICIA
What the evidence of the RCSP survey has revealed is that a Hellenistic horizon of ceramic remains is ­consistent
throughout the region, but the numbers are minimal in quantity and indicate a shallow pattern of small, d
­ ispersed
settlements. As the published context ceramics of the survey indicate (Autret et al. 2019), counts of H
­ ellenistic
ceramics in the survey region were limited (6%, or 339 out of some 5418 dated sherds). It is not so much their
numbers as it is their distribution that seems significant. Hellenistic ceramics were encountered in every region
that has been investigated, including the coastal sites and ridges investigated in 1996–1999, the Adanda Canyon
in the mesogeia investigated in 2000–2003 and the highland sites in the upper Bickici river basin investigated in
2003–2011. One highland site, Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), seems particularly noteworthy, because it sits at 1600 m
elevation, overlooking the pass that connects the Bickici River on the coast to the southern branch of the Göksu
or Calycadnus River on the interior. Moreover, Hellenistic ceramics were encountered at every categorized
locus, regardless of scale, from the large urban sites such as Iotape and Selinus, to village scale settlements, to
isolated farmsteads, kiln sites and press complexes, to random rural survey units. As we have noted previously,
the presence of pre-Roman ceramics at Iotape and Antiochia ad Cragum (Fig. 3) seems particularly important,
because both communities were established in the mid-1st century CE by the Roman client king Antiochus
IV of Commagene. What the pre-Roman pottery indicates, therefore, is that local settlements preceded these
foundations, settlements that may possibly have served as pirate bases.

variations, undoubtedly linked to the ancient name of Phournoi, often coexist with variants of the name
“Phournoi”. ­Conversely, from the 18th century onwards, variants of the name “Phournoi” appear to prevail
among ­cartographers.
The Latin transliteration of the ancient Greek name and its variants closely resemble the byzantine term for the
act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras
1982, s.v. κούρσο(ν), κούρσος) and correlate with derivatives of the Italian term corsario, loosely ­translated as
“one who has a license to raid” (letter de course), derived from Medieval Latin term cursarius (­“pirate”, from
Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of
the ancient name of Phournoi and the various terms for loot and corsair in Latin languages and medieval Greek
has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),
­Kleftolimano (harbor of thieves), Fygou (escape), Fylakio (guard-post), Vardia (shift or guard), Tourkolimnionas
(harbor of the Turks), Pano and Kato Maneta (upper and lower Maneta). Many of these names are commonplace along the Aegean coastline and are also encountered on other islands historically associated with piracy.
However, the two bays designated as Pano and Kato Maneta, situated roughly in the middle of the eastern coast
of the main island of Phournoi, warrant further comment.
It is highly probable that these two bays derived their names from the Zakynthian corsair Eustathios ­(Stathis)
Romanos or Manetas, who, between 1678 and 1684, operated as a pirate in the Aegean Sea while based in Melos,
commanding the only Greek privately owned corsair vessel at the time, most probably handed to him after the
death of its former owner, the Maltese corsair Hugues Creviliers (Krantonelli 1994, 289–91). Early records of
his exploits date back to 1683, when the rector of Tenos reported that Stathis Romanos Manetas had seized the
Venetian consul in Paros, extorting a monopoly over the supply of galette to Venetian fleet vessels. In May 1684,
Admiral Gerolamo Cornaro courted him on behalf of the Venetians, granting him a free pass permit (salvocondotto). Manetas subsequently conducted operations across the Aegean, Ionian and southern Adriatic, either
independently or in collaboration with the Venetians and the Knights of Malta (Krantonelli 1991, 300). At
the onset of the 6th Venetian-Turkish war (1684–1699), Morosini appointed him commander of the V
­ enetian
cruiser flotilla, where he actively participated in the sieges of Lefkada and Preveza (Sathas 1869, 312–19; Donos
2007, 74–85, 101). Subsequently, he assisted the Venetian admiral in levying taxes on Aegean islands and aiding
in the sieg

have overlooked. Manetas is etched into the popular consciousness due to his tumultuous personal life. Legend
has it that he married the beautiful Marioga in Melos, leaving her under the care of the island’s bishop when
he embarked on a pirate expedition. Marioga, steadfastly refusing the bishop’s advances, was falsely accused of
infidelity to Manetas. Subsequently, Manetas captured her and executed her at his place of business. This tragic
episode forms the central theme of “Manetas’ rhyme”, a popular Aegean folk song known in various renditions
today (Legrand 1874, 296–300; Spyridakis and Petropoulos 1962, 375–78; Poulianos 1964, 121–24). While each
version features adaptations of hero names and locales, the Ikarian rendition places Manetas’s attempt “in the
straits of Samos” (stes Samos ta boghazia), with his wife’s murder purportedly occurring there. Accordingly,
local traditions suggest that the murder took place either in Ikaria or Phournoi, specifically in the bays of Pano
and Kato Maneta. Nonetheless, whether Stathis Romanos Manetas utilized Phournoi as a base and secure anchorage during his operations in the Chios area in 1694 and 1695 remains a conjecture. Offspring of Manetas
continued the family tradition, engaging in acts of piracy for the most part of the first half of the 18th century
(Krantonelli 1998, 35–8, 168–69).

Rome responded to the piracy threat by enacting the Gabinian Law in 67 BCE, granting extraordinary
powers to the outgoing consul Gnaeus Pompey to eradicate piracy throughout the Mediterranean. Pompey’s
campaign, meticulously planned and brief, relied heavily on diplomacy rather than outright armed conflict and
proved highly effective.
Unlike Pharmakoussa, which gained notoriety due to a prominent incident, Phournoi never attracted
­significant attention from ancient historians. To uncover tangible evidence of pirate activity in Phournoi, one
must turn to the late Byzantine and post-Byzantine periods.
The earliest account mentioning Phournoi as an ambush site for Turkish pirates targeting merchant vessels
comes from the Florentine monk Cristoforo Buondelmonti in the early 15th century, who was shipwrecked
on the island and endured five days without food before being rescued by a passing ship (Buondelmonti 1897,
109–10 no. 55). Buondelmonti also noted the favorable anchorages provided by Phournoi, where ships could
seek shelter at night to avoid strong winds. However, he observed the island as deserted and abandoned by its
inhabitants. Apparently, its use by Turkish pirates was seasonal, a pattern recurring over the centuries.
Historical records indicate that during the latter half of the 15th century, the Genoese administration
­ rchestrated a mass relocation of the population of Samos to Chios, primarily due to piracy thriving in neigho
boring islands and Phournoi (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 158–59). Ottoman admiral Piri Reis also
depicted a similar scene of desolation at the beginning of the 16th century (Bülent 2002, 157). The abandonment described by Buondelmonti and Piri Reis seemingly rendered Phournoi an ideal refuge for various bands
of pirates to regroup and distribute their plunder.
In the summer of 1602, the Spanish pirate Alonso de Contreras sought refuge on the deserted islands
of Phournoi with his Maltese frigate and companions, following a series of successful operations in Serifos,
­Astypalaia, Amorgos and Patmos, intending to regroup and divide their spoils. However, they were compelled
to abandon the islands when two galleys under Suleiman of Catania, then Bey of Chios, appeared, forcing de
Contreras to flee via Ikaria and Mykonos (Durant 1975, 146–56; Krantonelli 1991, 107–9, 333; de Contreras
1994, 97–102).
The involvement of corsairs from the Order of the Knights of St. John of Malta and other Christian forces in
the Archipelago of Phournoi is corroborated by the description of Ikaria by Joseph Georgirenes, the archbishop
of Samos and Ikaria, published in London in 1677, reflecting his experiences in the early 1670s (Georgirenes
1677, 3–4, 55; Papalas 2002, 258–67). Georgirenes notes the uninhabited islets of Phournoi, located three miles
south of the coast of Ikaria, boasting natural harbors capable of accommodating various vessels. He further
mentions that at other times, corsairs from Malta and other Christian factions would lie in wait on these islands,
ambushing ships trading between Chios and Rhodes.
The daily routine of these corsair groups is vividly described by the English captive Mr. Roberts, who was
shipwrecked in Ios in 1692 and subsequently captured by pirates, forced to serve as a gunner on their ship.
­According to Roberts, the corsairs would spend the winter in Paros, Antiparos, Melos and Ios until early March.
They would then relocate to Phournoi, where they would lie in wait from early spring to mid-summer, with
lookouts stationed in the mountains overlooking the Samos-Ikaria strait, keeping watch for passing ships. They
would also venture into the southern part of Ikaria, Gaidouronisi and Leipsoi, before moving further south to
posts in Asia Minor, spanning from Cilicia to Cyprus. In autumn, they would return to the Aegean to sell their
plunder and deliver profits to their backers in Livorno, Malta or Marseille (Hacke 1699; Ormerod 1924, 17–8;
Krantonelli 1991, 89–93; Simopoulos 1994, 106).
This cyclic movement of ambush, aligned with the routes of convoys between Alexandria and C
­ onstantinople
or guided by intelligence from captured vessels, was undoubtedly a prevalent method of piracy during this era.
Similar tactics were employed by Jacopo Inghirami, the admi

certain ­anchorages would then become their safe havens and bases of operation.
Based on the above, is it possible for one to detect traces of the pirate phenomenon on land? We will attempt
to answer this question by focusing on the period of the extended Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century
(1645–1669, 1684–1699). In doing so, we will not concentrate on traces of material destruction related to the

MAINTENANCE OF THE PIRATE AND CORSAIR SHIPS
As already pointed out, pirate and corsair operations were interrupted from time to time to cater for the
­maintenance and supply needs of the ships. The success of the operations, after all, heavily depended on the
speed of sailing, which could only be ensured by regular maintenance of the keel, scraping it clean from marine
organisms and coating it with a mixture of grease and tar. These particular jobs, namely careening and graving,
were carried out at least twice a year. Another job that took place at regular but less frequent intervals was
caulking, namely the sealing of the hull with a tar-soaked oakum.
In order to complete all these maintenance operations, the ship had to be disarmed in a suitable cove (Jal
1848, 388–89, 423, 655–56; Jurien de La Gravière 1885, 219–20; Fennis 1995, 454, 491–92, 849–50). In the case
of pirates and corsairs, the cove in question had to fulfill a number of conditions in order to be considered
suitable. First, it had to allow the ship to approach the shore as far as possible; then, it had to be secluded, and,
finally, it had to provide opportunities for defense during the works, which we shall discuss below. The German
scholar Johann Michael Wansleben, who traveled in the Ottoman territories in the 1670s, notes in one of his
manuscripts that the corsairs graved their ships during the winter months in Astypalaia and Ios, while in June
and July in Porto Chevalier (Fethiye or Şövalye Adası) and one other anchorage on the coast of Lycia (BNF, MS
NAF 4193, f. 195v).1 Other sources, however, attest that the corsairs maintained their ships on Ios, Melos (­ Gazette
1668, 650, 660; Argenti 1954, 152) and evidently on other islands even during the summer months. I­ n­deed, a
text containing comments on maps of the Archipelago informs us that sometimes the corsairs careened their
ships at Arkioi (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 4), in the wider area of which, as we have already ­mentioned, they lay
in wait to ambush passing ships from spring until early summer.
1 I am grateful to my colleague Alastair Hamilton for pointing out this unpublished note by J.M. Wansleben.

The abovementioned bays are characterized by either a narrow entrance or one blocked by an islet, which
allowed the placement of cannons at the edges of the bay and/or on the islet to prevent enemy ships from
­approaching during maintenance work. This was a common defensive practice that was not only followed by the
Catholic corsairs. For example, in 1681, it is reported that, when corsairs from Tripoli in Libya were informed
that a French squadron was pursuing them and intended to attack them in Chios, they made plans to take refuge
in Nea Phocaea (Yenifoça), in order to maintain their ships and place cannons at the entrance of its harbor
(Argenti 1954, 164, 166, 175). What interests us here, however, is not the practice per se, but the construction of
defensive works for the placement of cannons in sites frequented by corsairs. Indeed, French portolans inform
us that, in the gulf of Melos, at the cape of Patrikia, the corsairs had constructed “a fort” (un fort) or, at least,
“something like a fort” (comme une espèce de fort) to install their cannons (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 5, 22 and
no. 8, 49). Roberts also attests that in the gulf of Naoussa, right on the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi, the corsairs had
constructed “a small battery” for the same purpose (Hacke 1699, 47).

LOOKOUTS
Beyond the installation of cannons in the bays, where the corsairs found refuge for the maintenance of their
ships, another practice, which may have left its traces in the landscape of the Archipelago, is the lookouts they
placed on the highest points around the bays they used, either as ambush points or shipyards (Earle 2010, 158).
In the 17th century, this practice is attested in Ios (Gazette 1668, 652–53; Argenti 1954, 152), in Pharmakonissi
(de Contreras 1977, 67), and, of course, in Phournoi (Hacke 1699, 8), where even today the names of the island’s
bays indicate that they were once the lairs of famous corsairs: Pano and Kato Maneta bays and, possibly, Pavlos
bay (Fig. 9).
The sentries alerted the corsairs to the appearance of ships in the distance by hoisting or waving small flags,
thus giving orders to prepare for defensive or raiding operations. This practice should probably be associated
with the name Bandieres (or Padieres) of the hill on the south side of the bay of Vathy, as the present-day
­inhabitants of Astypalaia do not have any explanation for this place name (Fig. 2). Thus, the name of the hill is
probably not related to the relatively recent Italian occupation of the island, but to the practices of sailors of an
earlier time (Koutzakiotis 2023, 231–32).
Moreover, it is no coincidence that a similar place name is found in the narrow strait between Antiparos and
Paros, where corsair ships frequently anchored. More specifically, the southernmost islet of the strait is called
Pandieronissi and, as it is the largest of a cluster of islets and skerries, it lends its name to the entire cluster:
Pandieronissia (Fig. 1). It must be added here that one of the Pandieronissia bears the name Preza (Skandalidis
2001, 185), which in the lingua franca of the time denoted the spoils of corsairs or pirates, their “prize”. “Preza”
as a micro-toponym is also encountered today in Kimolos (Katsouros 1975, 326).

claims.acquired_text_excerpt:
Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis
Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted VenetianOttoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

When Paul I came to the throne in 1796, Malta and Russia had long had
a common enemy. It was the Ottoman Empire, its Muslim Turks, and
its Barbary corsairs. Unlike Malta, a central Mediterranean archipelago
with well-protected, deep-water harbours, Russia had been a largely
landlocked country whose territorial expansion historically had tended
to be across internal frontiers, from Kiev to Muscovy to Kazan. With the
advent of Peter I, however, and especially after his declaration of war
against Turkey and the acquisition of the Black Sea port of Azov in 1696,
Russia began to nurture a naval and maritime policy. This policy was
two-pronged: to the North in the struggle with Sweden for access to the
Baltic; to the South in the long drawn out confrontations with the Turks
in their extensive domains, hemming Russia in from the Mediterranean,
and indeed from the Black Sea.
Paul I's keen interest in Malta and its Catholic, aristocratic order
of chivalry, must be seen in the light of a string of earlier acquaintances,
overtures and schemes of mutual interest between the Czars of
Russia, on one hand, and the Knights of Malta, on the other. Two of
his best known predecessors, Peter I (1672-1725) and Catherine II
(1729-1796), already had set their sights on Malta, its knights and, not
least, its famous fleet. Given the new-found commitment to naval and
maritime undertakings, Petrine Russia now had an ideological as well
as a strategic shared interest with the Mediterranean headquarters of
the anti-Turkish, anti-Muslim crusaders.
From Russia's point of view, this interest was also technical and
. professional, in so far as the successful equipment, organization and
the leadership of its own Russian fleet was concerned. This made
sense, too, in the context of the Western expertise and support which
both Peter and Catherine sought, coveted and to an extent emulated,
The founding editor of Storja in 1978, Henry Frendo has taught in various universities and is the author
of several books; since 1992 he has been Professor of History at the University of Malta.

research_answer.question:
Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο (1600-1700)
Research scope: Νέα πραγματική αναζήτηση πηγών για ορμητήρια, αγκυροβόλια και καταφύγια πειρατών και κουρσάρων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο, 1600–1700. Αναζήτησε σε όλες τις έντεκα οικογένειες πηγών, περιηγητές, portolans, σύγχρονα κείμενα, αρχεία και μεταγενέστερες μελέτες. Απόκτησε τα προσβάσιμα πραγματικά κείμενα. Για κάθε εύρημα δώσε ιστορικό τοπωνύμιο, σύγχρονη ταύτιση και γεωγραφική θέση μόνο όπου τεκμηριώνονται, χρονολογία, χρήστες, είδος χρήσης, ακριβή πηγή, σελίδα ή φύλλο ή αρχειακή αναφορά, ακριβές απόσπασμα, confidence και verification status. Ξεχώρισε αναφορά πηγής, ερμηνεία και υπόθεση, μεταγενέστερη μελέτη από πρωτογενές τεκμήριο και ορμητήριο από τόπο επιδρομής. Μην μετατρέπεις τη χρονολογία του ερωτήματος σε χρονολογία αχρονολόγητου γεγονότος. Δήλωσε απρόσιτα αρχεία και ανεξέταστο υλικό. Καμία αυτόματη ιστορική επαλήθευση.

Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis
Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted VenetianOttoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

evidence.text:
CHURCHES
Despite the atrocities they committed, pirates and corsairs, like their contemporaries, never forgot the divine
­element and manifested their religiosity in various ways, either because they had genuine metaphysical concerns
or simply for reasons of social prestige and/or alliances with the religious authorities. The historical notes of
the Capuchin monks of Naxos, which also narrate events from the period under consideration, record, among
other things, donations from corsairs to the local Catholic Church, which were subsequently used by the clergy
to build and equip temples; these included captives (to be exchanged for ransom), sums of money, precious
vessels, textiles and quantities of metals (Zerlentis 1922).
The role of the corsairs in church-building, however, was not always discreet and indirect. The Vitali coat of
arms, which was mentioned earlier, bears at the bottom an inscription in Latin, which informs us that he was
the founder of the church of “Spyridon, the miracle worker” (Fig. 7). He probably erected the church after he
was spared from a plague epidemic, if we take into account the relevant traditions about this particular saint.
A second case of a church built by a corsair is found in the closed sea surrounded by Melos, Kimolos and
Polyaigos, which is interrupted by two straits, and where corsair ships frequently anchored, as, much like in the
strait of Antiparos, no enemy ship could entrap them (BSB, Cod. gall. 728, 77; Sebastiani 1687, 29). More specifically, from a study by the priest Ioannis Ramphos (1932, 31–52), we now know that the small monastery of
Ayios Georgios on the islet of the same name (Ayios Georgios, which was called Ayionissi until the 19th century)
was always Orthodox (Fig. 1). The surviving patriarchal sigils certify as early as 1700 that it had been erected
from the ground up by the grandfather of the then abbot on the previously deserted islet.
Ramphos, however, cannot explain why the church is presented externally as a two-aisled basilica, while
it is lacking in internal unity, adding that the right building of this essentially twin church was called by the
­Kimolians “Frangokklisia” (Ramphos 1932, 43–4). The local tradition of the Frankish origins of the church is
ultimately verified by the records of the French consulate of Melos, which refer to a 1695 decision of capitan
generale Antonio Zeno, acknowledging that the Tuscan corsair Francesco Barbieri had built a Catholic church
honoring Saint George in Ayionissi (CADN, Milo et l’Argentière 3, 216).

evidence.text:
PIRACY ACTIVITIES OF GARP OCAKLARI IN MEDITERRANEAN WORLD
ACCORDING TO GENOESE ARCHIVE DOCUMENTS (1665-1690)
Abstract
The damage of Western merchants departing from Ottoman ports, especially Izmir and Istanbul, and the confiscation
of their property by pirates have caused serious problems with European states. Mediterranean piracy, which began
to increase in the second half of the 16th century and peaked in the last quarter, continued in the 17th century. In the
second half of the 17th century, the Ottomans had to deal not only with the Venetians in the Battle of Crete, but also
with problems related to attacks on the ships of some Western merchants by pirates. In our study, an assessment will
be made on examples of the fact that some of the British, Venetian, Genoese, Dutch and French commercial ships
operating from the Ottoman ports where trade gained intensity in the second half of the 17th century were exposed to
attacks by pirates before Algeria, Tunisia and Tripoli in the Mediterranean, their property was confiscated by them
and its effects on bilateral relations between Western states and Ottomans. The main source of our study will be the
letters of embassies and consuls belonging to the Genoa State Archive, their reports, and the registers in the Collection
of State Papers in the British State Archive. The study will also benefit from correspondences of especially those who
served in Izmir in the second half of the 17th century such as Agostino Spinola, Durazzo, Sinibaldo Fieschi, Pompeo
Giustiniani and Ottavio Doria, Luigi Cartabono, Simon Massa and Giovanni Luigi Gentile.
Keywords: Ottoman Empire, Western Colonies, Piracy, Venice, Genoese

suitable for the war as waged by corsairs. Its firing
capacity must have served solely to distract the enemy
vessel and make boarding easier since it was important
to make the largest number of men prisoners, and
therefore slaves, and take possession of the ship's
cargo. The sinking of lln enemy ship was not the
primary objective of the galley at war. 3
A feature of the big galleys used in Mediterranean
warfare during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries
was the enormous complement they carried, not
infrequently approaching five hundred men, sometimes
reaching even the six hundred mark. Apart from a
nucleus of about twenty-five knights and serving
brothers, each galley of the Order carried a mixed
complement of sailors, rowers and homini
d' armamento (soldiers). The galera Capitana, as a
rule, carried more men than other galleys including
some thirty knights; its compliment of both s.ailors
and homini d'armamento varied with time. In 1618
the Capitana carried a crew of one hundred and eighty
men together with 160 hemini d'armamento, 4

If we want to generalize this conclusion, however, we have to locate, collect
and study more sources coming from this milieu of seamen, Muslim or Christian.
As far as I know, all known Ottoman texts on seafaring come from a different
milieu, that of admirals and geographers. Seydi Ali Reis, for instance, the admiral
of the Indian Ocean in mid-sixteenth century, describes his wanderings in the
Indian Ocean in a somewhat similar yet ultimately different way: although he,
too, seems not to mention in his text the points of the compass as geographical
indicators (though he does mention the use of compass per se), it is clear that he
has in mind a mental map with places such as Diu, Hormuz or Yemen dispersed
in space, and which he uses in order to indicate the position and movements of
his fleet.40 That is to say, his perception of the Ocean is based on a grid composed
by orientated places rather than routes, as our anonymous author’s perception
seems to be. Almost one century later, in his introduction to the naval history
of the Ottomans, Kâtip Çelebi gives a description of the Eastern Mediterranean
using the cardinal points,41 before narrating the movements of the Ottoman fleet.
Moreover, Kâtip Çelebi systematically uses mileage instead of time units for distances, mainly between stable points and even when giving advice to future corsairs.42 Of course, this less than cursory inspection of sources is not adequate to
reach conclusions on the perception of the Mediterranean. However, I think the
difference between our anonymous author and educated geographers who know
the use of a complete map is evident.

ABSTRACT
The pirate phenomenon in the Aegean –and generally in the Mediterranean– is inscribed in the longue durée and formed
an economic activity that was not always illegal. Nevertheless, the difficulty to detect its traces is a commonplace among
historians and archaeologists. This paper attempts to respond to this challenge by focusing on the period of the extended
Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century (1645–1669, 1684–1699). During this period, the pirate phenomenon, in its
corsair version, was manifested with particular intensity in the Aegean and was normalized. The normalcy with which
corsairing was vested is fragmentarily attested in various types of contemporary sources, and still echoes to this day in the
collective memory of islanders and the microtoponymy of the Archipelago. These testimonies, though few in number, show
that various monuments and architectural remains in the island complexes of the Aegean are or could be linked with the
needs of the corsairs to defend themselves, guard their captives, heal their bodies and strive for the salvation of their souls.

THE ANNUAL CYCLE OF CATHOLIC CORSO
Various sources of the last three decades of the 17th century inform us that the activity of Catholic corsairs in the
Eastern Mediterranean followed an annual cycle, which was imposed by weather conditions and, ­consequently,
by the schedule of the Ottoman fleet. The fleet of Kapudan Pasha sailed in the Aegean to collect taxes from the
islands only when the weather was favorable, between the feast of Saint George and the feast of Saint Demetrius
(Hidrellez and Kasim respectively in Islam). More specifically, the corsairs acted as follows:
During the winter months, from mid-December until March or, according to another source (Deloffre and
Rougeot 1976, 233), until the end of April, they retreated to islands of the southern Aegean, where no Ottomans resided, mainly Melos, Kimolos, Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Astypalaia (Fig. 1). In the spring, the corsairs boarded their ships and headed eastwards to Phournoi and their environs, between Ikaria, Agathonisi
and Leipsoi, where, until the first summer months, they would ambush ships following the Asia Minor route,
namely those that sailed through the passage between the Dodecanese and the Asia Minor coast that connected
the ports of Syria-Palestine and Alexandria with Smyrna and Constantinople. Around the middle of July, they
sailed along the coast of Cyprus and, as soon as they received the slightest news about the presence of Algerian
or Ottoman vessels in Rhodes, they would head for the coasts of Alexandria and Damietta, where the shallow
waters would prevent these vessels from approaching. Around the end of the summer, the corsairs would approach the Syrian coast, where they could disembark their ships and go ashore in feluccas, capturing people in
and releasing them for ransom. In the autumn, they would return to the Aegean, where they would continue
their operations until the advent of winter (ANF, A.E. BI 862, f. 75v; Magni 1679, 292–95; Hacke 1699, 8–9).

Le journal de Thomas Baker donne une idée de la place 
qu’occupaient les esclaves dans l’économie du butin que les cor¬ 
saires musulmans tiraient des navires. Le plus frappant, dans ces 
listes des prises ramenées à Tripoli entre 1679 et 1685 est, nous 
l’avons déjà noté, le nombre très important de vaisseaux capturés 
sans le moindre esclave : sur les 71 bateaux pris lors de ces six 
années, seuls 30, soit environ les trois cinquièmes, le furent avec 
des captifs ; pour les autres, les équipages et les passagers avaient 
tous pris la fuite dans de petites embarcations lorsqu’il n’avait 
plus fait le moindre doute qu’ils ne pourraient pas distancer les 
corsaires. L’abandon du navire semble avoir été une réaction 
assez courante aux attaques pirates en Méditerranée, un acte en 
tout cas que Baker semble avoir considéré comme la seule chose 
raisonnable à faire. Notant que bien des prises étaient ramenées 
sans hommes parce que « tous les chrétiens avaient eu le bon 
sens de s’échapper », Baker semble convenir avec les équipages 
que rester combattre et risquer sa vie ou une existence de servi¬ 
tude simplement pour protéger les intérêts de propriétaires restés 
à l’abri chez eux à Londres, Amsterdam ou Marseille, n’avait pas 
grand sens.

evidence.text:
Cela dit, les navires marchands restaient la cible favorite de la 
plupart des corsaires en opération après 1700. À lui seul, le volume 
du trafic en Méditerranée exerçait sur les pirates un attrait irrésis¬ 
tible et, comme le fit remarquer Braudel, la prospérité que connut 
la piraterie entre Gibraltar et le Levant peut être considérée comme 
un indice de la vitalité économique de la région autant que du 
désordre politique qui y régnait 66 . Les navires marchands étaient 
dans l’ensemble des proies bien plus faciles que tes cibles terrestres, 
notamment parce qu’il était trop difficile de coordonner un trafic 
commercial aussi important. Les capitaines des vaisseaux, trouvant 
malaisé ou peu pratique de rester groupés en convoi, rechignaient 
souvent à veiller les uns sur les autres; du coup, les corsaires tom¬ 
baient constamment sur des vaisseaux isolés en haute mer et mal 
protégés. Grâce à leurs galères équipées de rames, les corsaires 
pouvaient se précipiter sur des navires encalminés dans les eaux 
imprévisibles de la Méditerranée; grâce à leurs rapides fiistes gréées 
de voiles latines ils pouvaient espérer rattraper tous les navires 
marchands, sauf peut-être les plus petits et légers. Comme nous 
l’avons vu, les équipages chrétiens préféraient souvent abandonner 
le navire plutôt que de risquer la capture et l’asservissement, mais 
ceux qui étaient prêts à se battre pouvaient causer de sérieux pro¬ 
blèmes à leurs agresseurs, et plus d’une galère corsaire rentra au 
port bredouille et sévèrement malmenée par ses « victimes » 67 .

CENEVİZ ARŞİV BELGELERİNE GÖRE GARP OCAKLARININ AKDENİZDEKİ
KORSANLIK FAALİYETLERİ (1665-1690)
Selim PARLAZ
Öz
İzmir ve İstanbul başta olmak üzere Osmanlı limanlarından hareket eden Batılı tüccarların zarara uğratılması ve
korsanlar tarafından mallarına el konulması Avrupalı devletlerle ciddi problemlere yol açmıştır. XVI. yüzyılın ikinci
yarısında artmaya başlayan ve son çeyreğinde zirve yapan Akdeniz korsanlığı XVII. yüzyılda da devam etmiştir.
Osmanlılar XVII. yüzyılın ikinci yarısında Girit Savaşı’nda yalnız Venediklilerle değil, korsanlar tarafından bazı
Batılı tüccarların gemilerine yapılan saldırılarla ilgili sorunlarla da uğraşmak zorunda kalmıştır. Çalışmamızda XVII.
yüzyılın ikinci yarısında ticaretin yoğunluk kazandığı Osmanlı limanlarından hareket eden İngiliz, Venedik, Ceneviz,
Hollanda ve Fransa ticari gemilerinden bazılarının Akdeniz’de Cezayir, Tunus ve Trablusgarp önlerinde korsanların
saldırılarına maruz kalmaları, onlar tarafından mallarına el konulmaları ve bunun Batılı devletlerle Osmanlılar
arasındaki ikili ilişkilere etkileri hakkında örnekler üzerinden bir değerlendirme yapılacaktır. Çalışmamızın temel
kaynağını Cenova Devlet Arşivi’ne ait elçilik ve konsolos mektupları, raporları ile İngiliz Devlet Arşivi’ndeki State
Papers kolleksiyonunda bulunan defterler teşkil edecektir. Özellikle XVII. yüzyılın ikinci yarısında İstanbul’da görev
yapan Agostino Spinola, Durazzo, Sinibaldo Fieschi, Pompeo Giustiniani ile İzmir’de görev yapan Ottavio Doria,
Luigi Cartabono, Simon Massa ve Giovanni Luigi Gentile’nin yazışmalarından istifade edilecektir.
Anahtar Kelimeler: Osmanlı Devleti, Garp Ocakları, Korsanlık, Venedik, Ceneviz

evidence.text:
Yukarıdaki ifadelerden çıkarılabilecek önemli hususlardan biri Cenevizliler nezdinde Garp
Ocaklarının varlığı ve etkisi üzerinedir. Her birinin ayrı ayrı özellikleri ortaya konularak dikkat
edilmesi gereken hususlar üzerinde durulmaktadır. Böylece merkezlerini devamlı şekilde dikkatli
olunması konusunda uyarmaktadırlar. Çünkü, Osmanlılar için özellikle Batı ve Orta Akdeniz
özelinde Garp Ocaklarının varlığı son derece önemli bir yer tutmaktadır. Osmanlıların gerek
Cenevizlilerle gerekse de diğer Avrupa devletleri ile ilişkilerinde denizlerde çok önemli bir rol
oynamaktadırlar. Korsanlık hareketlerinin seyri ve ikili ilişkilerdeki yeri Cenevizlilerin takip
ettikleri hususlar arasındadır.
Yukarıda ifade edildiği üzere korsan saldırılarına hemen hemen her devletin gemileri maruz
kalıyordu. Bu eylem bazen gemi içindeki mallara ve techizata el konulması bazen de mürettebatın
esir edilmesi ve geminin batırılması suretiyle son buluyordu. Bu örnekleri daha da çoğaltmak
mümkündür. Ancak resmin bütününü aydınlatan örnekler üzerinden değerlendirme yapmak
konunun daha net anlaşılmasını sağlamaktadır.
Sonuç olarak çeyrek asırlık bir dönemi ele alan bu çalışmanın gösterdiği üzere Venedik’in
ihtişamlı dönemi biterken İngiltere, Fransa ve Hollanda devletlerinin yükselişi başlamaktadır.
Garp Ocakları korsanlarının saldırıları Atlantik ülkelerinin gemileri üzerinde yoğunlaşmaya
başlamıştır. Ceneviz kaynaklarına dayalı olan bu çalışmada doğal olarak Garp Ocaklarının
Ceneviz ile ilişkilerine daha fazla yer verilmiştir. Ancak gerek Girit Savaşı sırasında gerekse
sonrasında Garp Ocaklarının faaliyetlerine yoğun bir şekilde devam ettikleri görülmüştür. Savaş
sırasında bir taraftan Osmanlı Devleti’ne yardımcı olurken diğer taraftan da asli işlerine yani
korsanlığa devam etmişlerdir.

evidence.text:
aktif bir şekilde mücadelenin içerisinde bulunmaları önemli bir etkendi. Osmanlılara karşı
Venediklilerle birlikte hareket eden Fransızların Doğu Akdeniz ve adalarda, Osmanlı limanlarında
sıkıntıya girmeleri normal bir sonuçtu. Bu sıkıntının ana nedenlerinden biri de 1665 yılında Fransız
elçisi Denis De La Haye’in muhalefetine rağmen Girit Savaşı sırasında Ceneviz elçisi Agostino
Durazzo’ya verilen kapitülasyonlardı. Bu durumun üstüne Garp Ocakları korsanlarının Fransız
gemilerine saldırmaları21 ve el koymaları da eklenince sıkıntıları bir kat daha arttı. İstanbul ve
İzmir gibi bazı Osmanlı limanlarından hareket eden Fransız gemileri korsan saldırıları nedeniyle
Marsilya ve diğer limanlara giderken zor anlar yaşamaktaydı. Nitekim, 11 Şubat 1673 tarihinde
Cenevizlilerin Sakız adasındaki konsolosları Ottaviano Giustiniani, İzmir’deki Luigi Gentile’ye
gönderdiği mektupta, Sakız adasında Marsilya’ya doğru giden Fransız gemilerine rastladığını
belirtmektedir. Ancak bu gemilerin daha sonra Doğu Akdeniz’deki Milos (Milo) adası sularında
Venedik bayrağı altında 4 Cezayir Garp Ocağı korsanının gemisiyle karşılaştığını, sadrazamın
Tunus ve Trablusgarb birlikleriyle beraber bölgeye nüfuz ettiğini, Cezayirlilerin uzun zamandır
bu sularda durakladıklarını yazmaktadır. Tunus’ta da 4 kadırganın bu birliklerle bir araya geldiğini
sayının 12’ye ulaştığını belirtmektedir (ASG. 2703, 11 Şubat 1673).
Fransız gemilerinin en çok muzdarip olduğu ve tasalluta maruz kaldıkları yerlerden biri de Doğu
Akdeniz’de Sakız adası ve çevresidir. Örneğin, 12 Haziran 1674 tarihinde İzmir’deki Konsolos
Giovanni Luigi Gentile’nin Cenova hükümetine gönderdiği mektuba göre Sakız adasında biri
Tunus’lu ve biri Trablusgarb’lı olmak üzere toplam 16 korsan gemisinden oluşan iki filo
bulunmaktadır. Korsanlar, Sakız adasından çıkan ve buraya giren tüccar gemilerine büyük zararlar
vermektedir. Hatta Fransa’nın Akdeniz’deki en önemli limanı olan Marsilya şehrinden İstanbul’a
giden Diamante adlı Fransız gemisi korkudan geri dönmek zorunda kalmaktadır22. Benzer şekilde
Gentile’nin bir başka raporunda da İzmir’den İskenderiye’ye hareket eden Fransız Asia adlı gemi
Sakız sularında Trablusgarb korsanları nedeniyle bekletilmektedir (ASG. 2703, 6 Şubat 1673).
Fransız ticaret gemileri Osmanlı topraklarına birçok mal taşıdığı gibi onları alıp Akdeniz ile Fransa
ve İtalya limanlarına da sevk etmektedir. Ancak bazen Tunus korsanları nedeniyle bu durum
aksamalara neden olmaktadır. Mesela, 23 Kasım 1670 tarihinde Benzert’ten (Bizerte) ayrılan 5
Tunuslu korsan gemisi, Trablusşam’dan Livorno’ya doğru yola çıkan değerli eşyalarla yüklü bir
Fransız barçasını Monte Christo adası açıklarında ele geçirmektedir (SP. 120/14, 23 Kasım 1670).
Benzer şekilde İzmir’deki elçi Carlo Massa’nın 14 Eylül 1674 tarihli raporuna göre de mezkur
şehirden Venedik’e doğru hareket etmek üzere olan ve kaptanlığını Grasiglia’nın yaptığı bir
Fransız gemisi, adalardaki Tunus gemilerinin yollarına çıkabilme endişesi ve kaygısı nedeniyle
burada beklemek zorunda kalmaktadır (ASG. 2703, 14 Eylül 1674).

Bu çalışmanın esasını Archivio di Stato di Genova yani Cenova Devlet Arşivi’ndeki İtalyanca

evidence.text:
Hollanda ticaret gemileri Osmanlı topraklarına birçok mal taşıdığı gibi onları alıp Akdeniz ve
İtalya limanlarına da sevk etmektedir. Bunu ise genelde Akdeniz’de yaygın bir biçimde
kullanıldığını gördüğümüz savaş gemilerinin refakatinde konvoy sistemiyle yapmaktadır.
Güvenlik sorunlarını aşma ya da en alt seviyeye indirme amacıyla uygulanan bu sistemin özellikle
Hollandalı tüccarlar tarafından yoğun bir şekilde uygulandığı bilinmektedir33. Ancak, bu durum
Trablusgarb korsanları nedeniyle bazen aksamalara neden olmaktadır. Örneğin, İzmir’deki Luigi
Gentile’nin 6 Şubat 1673 tarihli raporuna göre Osmanlı limanlarına34 doğru hareket etmek üzere
olan Hollanda gemileri, yoluna çıkabilecek güçlü ve donanımlı iki Trablusgarb gemisi şüphesi
nedeniyle İtalya’da beklemek zorunda kalmaktadır (ASG. 2703, 6 Şubat 1673).
XVII. yüzyılın son çeyreğinde de Garp Ocakları korsanlarının faaliyetleri devam etmektedir. Bu
bağlamda 1680 yılında Hollandalılara bir ahidname verilmiştir. Buna göre Cezayir-i Garp
korsanları Hollanda limanlarında elzem olan mühimmat ihtiyacını karşılarken mezkur korsanların
Hollandalı tüccarları esir etmeyerek emtiasını yağmalamayacakları kararı alınmıştır.
Garp ocakları korsanlarının XVII. yüzyılın ikinci yarısındaki faaliyetleri hakkında bilgi veren
kaynaklardan biri de Evliya Çelebi Seyahatnamesi’dir. Özellikle bizzat savaş için asker toplayarak
mücadeleye katılan seyyah Mora Yarımadası ve etrafında gelişen olaylara tanıklık etmiştir.
Bilhassa Cezayir korsanlarının deryada dolaşıp av ararlarken Holumiç35 Kalesi dağını seçip
Larinçe limanlarında demir attıklarını belirtmiştir (Evliya Çelebi, 2005: 131). Başka bir örnek
olarak da Cezayir ve Trablusgarb’dan 5 parça korsan levent gemisinin Moton Limanı yanında
Sipanca adası civarında içlerinde seksener adet top bulunan 2 Frenk kalyonuna el koymasını
vermiştir. Yazar, bu gemilerin Girit Adası’na mühimmat ve askerî yardım götürdüğünü belirtmiştir
(Evliya Çelebi, 2005: 144).
6. Sonuç
XVII. yüzyılın ikinci yarısında uzun bir süreyi kapsayan Girit Savaşı insanlık tarihi kadar eski olan
korsanlık faaliyetlerinin yoğunlaşmasına neden olan önemli gelişmelerden biriydi. Osmanlı
limanlarından hareket eden ya da bu limanlara doğru Avrupa kentlerinden emtia taşıyan bütün
gemiler açık bir tehdit halindeydi. Osmanlılar tarafından Avrupalı devletlere verilen ahidnâmelere
rağmen faaliyetler, hem savaş sırasında hem de sonrasında aynı şekilde devam etmekteydi.
Özellikle adalarda, Ege Denizi’nde ve Kuzey Afrika önlerinde korsanlık faaliyetleri oldukça
cüretkâr bir hal almıştı. Girit Savaşı’nın bitişiyle Akdeniz’de sükuneti sağlama yolunda önemli bir
adım atılsa da yüzyılın son çeyreğinde de korsanlık faaliyetleri devam etmekteydi. Alınan
tedbirler, yapılan antlaşmalar bu tür olayları engelleme ya da azaltma amacı taşısa da beklentiler
çoğu zaman karşılanamadı. Çünkü ganimet her türlü isteğin önünde yer almaktaydı. Garp ocakları
korsanlarını bu istekten ve de en iyi bildikleri işten vazgeçirmek hiç de kolay değildi.

sefinelerinden Specchio di Mar adlı gemi Venedik’ten peksimetleriyle yüklü olarak Suda
Kalesi’ne gitmiştir. Burada yüklerini boşaltan sefine için, Kandiye Eyâleti’ne mutasarrıf olan
İbrahim Paşa, Suda Limanı’nda olan gemiye dostluğa binaen İzmir’e gidecek askerleri olduğunu

askeri gemi ile İzmir’e gönderilmiştir. Sefine Rodos’a dâhil olduktan sonra Kıbrıs Beylerbeyisi

3. Fransızlar ile İlişkiler
Garp Ocakları korsanlarının saldırıları sadece Venedik ve Ceneviz ticaret gemileri ile tahdit
edilmiş değildi. Mezkur korsanlardan en çok muzdarip olan devletlerden biri de Fransızlar idi.
Korsanlık faaliyetleri Fransızların Akdeniz’deki ticaretini kesintiye uğratıyordu. XVII. yüzyılla
beraber Garp Ocakları’nın saldırıları daha da arttı. Bu olayların yaşanmasında özellikle yüzyılın
ilk yarısında başlayıp ikinci yarısında da devam eden Girit savaşı sırasında Fransız gemilerinin
Firkate, çekdiri türü donanma gemileri içinde en küçüğü on-on yedi oturaklı olan gemi türüdür. (Bostan, 2017: 139).

originaires de ces États étaient des proies légitimes — c’est ce qu’ils

attaqués 71 .

Du côté africain de la Méditerranée, la traite des esclaves 
laissa également des traces profondes, même si elles le furent 
moins que celles produites par la traite transatlantique en direc¬ 
tion des Amériques et si elles ne relevèrent pas en premier lieu 
de critères culturels ou raciaux. Bien que l’activité reproductrice 
des esclaves mâles fût soigneusement, et même farouchement 
contrôlée, les nombreuses captives européennes abusées par 
leurs maîtres et les milliers d’immigrants renégats apportèrent 
une bonne dose de sang européen au patrimoine génétique local. 
En outre, d’autres Européens d’origine jouirent longtemps de 
positions dominantes dans ces sociétés hors-la-loi, Alger par¬ 
ticulièrement. Les 20000 janissaires qui y formaient le coeur 
du pouvoir turc étaient par définition tous d’ascendance balka¬ 
nique; les couloglis qui résultèrent de leur union à des esclaves 
ou à des Maures furent si nombreux qu’ils constituaient une 
caste sociale à part entière dans la plupart des régences. 11 y 
eut également une élite de renégats extrêmement influente tout 
au long du siècle compris entre 1580 et 1680, encore une fois 
particulièrement à Alger. Les listes des raïs corsaires datant de 
cette période montrent clairement que plus de la moitié étaient 
d’origine européenne, des hommes qui en vinrent à exercer une 
emprise économique considérable sur des villes dont l’aisance 
dépendait de la piraterie !15 . Leur richesse et leur pouvoir firent 
de nombre d’entre eux des figures dominantes dans la culture 
locale; l’islam débraillé (quoique souvent acharné) qu’ils pra¬ 
tiquaient et la lingua jranca abâtardie qu’ils parlaient à leurs 
concitoyens eurent un impact durable sur les communautés 
métisses uniques en leur genre qui se développèrent et furent 
florissantes pendant plusieurs siècles au Maghreb.

Garp Ocakları korsanlarının faaliyetleri, İngiliz gemilerine de şamildi. İngiltere, 1580 tarihli
ahidnâme ile Tunus, Trablusgarb ve Cezayir iskelelerinde konsolos bulundurma hakkını elde
etmişti. Ayrıca bu ahidnâmeyle korsan gemilerinin İngilizleri esir edip satmaları da
yasaklanıyordu. İngiltere, Garp Ocaklarına barut, kurşun ve baharat satıyor, onlardan portakal,
limon, zeytin, zeytinyağı, üzüm, balmumu, yün, tuz vb. ürünler alıyordu. Bu emtiadan bazılarının
yabancılara satışı yasak olmasına rağmen, mühimmat karşılığında olduğundan izin veriliyordu
(Bostan, 1994: 65-68).
Ahidnâmelere rağmen 17. yüzyılın başlarında Cezayir korsanları sadece Akdeniz’de değil, Güney
İngiltere’ye kadar uzanan bölgede korsanlıkla büyük ganimetler ele geçiriyordu. Aynı zamanda
Akdeniz’e çıkan İngiliz tüccar gemilerini hedef alıyor, mallarını ele geçirdikleri gibi gemilerine el

de gönderilen fermanlar ya da yeniden yapılan anlaşmalara rağmen korsanlık sonlandırılamıyordu.
Nitekim, İngilizlere Sultan Osman devrinde verilen ikinci ahidnâmeye eklenen bir madde Garp

ve Cezayir korsanları, aldıkları malları sahiplerine iâde edecekler, hükme uymadıkları takdirde
Osmanlı liman ve iskelelerine, özellikle Tunus, Cezayir, Mora ve Koron iskelelerine
sokulmayacaklardır (Kütükoğlu, 2013: 35-36). Buna rağmen yüzyılın ikinci yarısında İngiliz savaş
ve ticaret gemilerinin Garp Ocakları korsanlarının tasallutuna maruz kaldıkları bilinmektedir.

evidence.text:
Rome responded to the piracy threat by enacting the Gabinian Law in 67 BCE, granting extraordinary
powers to the outgoing consul Gnaeus Pompey to eradicate piracy throughout the Mediterranean. Pompey’s
campaign, meticulously planned and brief, relied heavily on diplomacy rather than outright armed conflict and
proved highly effective.
Unlike Pharmakoussa, which gained notoriety due to a prominent incident, Phournoi never attracted
­significant attention from ancient historians. To uncover tangible evidence of pirate activity in Phournoi, one
must turn to the late Byzantine and post-Byzantine periods.
The earliest account mentioning Phournoi as an ambush site for Turkish pirates targeting merchant vessels
comes from the Florentine monk Cristoforo Buondelmonti in the early 15th century, who was shipwrecked
on the island and endured five days without food before being rescued by a passing ship (Buondelmonti 1897,
109–10 no. 55). Buondelmonti also noted the favorable anchorages provided by Phournoi, where ships could
seek shelter at night to avoid strong winds. However, he observed the island as deserted and abandoned by its
inhabitants. Apparently, its use by Turkish pirates was seasonal, a pattern recurring over the centuries.
Historical records indicate that during the latter half of the 15th century, the Genoese administration
­ rchestrated a mass relocation of the population of Samos to Chios, primarily due to piracy thriving in neigho
boring islands and Phournoi (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 158–59). Ottoman admiral Piri Reis also
depicted a similar scene of desolation at the beginning of the 16th century (Bülent 2002, 157). The abandonment described by Buondelmonti and Piri Reis seemingly rendered Phournoi an ideal refuge for various bands
of pirates to regroup and distribute their plunder.
In the summer of 1602, the Spanish pirate Alonso de Contreras sought refuge on the deserted islands
of Phournoi with his Maltese frigate and companions, following a series of successful operations in Serifos,
­Astypalaia, Amorgos and Patmos, intending to regroup and divide their spoils. However, they were compelled
to abandon the islands when two galleys under Suleiman of Catania, then Bey of Chios, appeared, forcing de
Contreras to flee via Ikaria and Mykonos (Durant 1975, 146–56; Krantonelli 1991, 107–9, 333; de Contreras
1994, 97–102).
The involvement of corsairs from the Order of the Knights of St. John of Malta and other Christian forces in
the Archipelago of Phournoi is corroborated by the description of Ikaria by Joseph Georgirenes, the archbishop
of Samos and Ikaria, published in London in 1677, reflecting his experiences in the early 1670s (Georgirenes
1677, 3–4, 55; Papalas 2002, 258–67). Georgirenes notes the uninhabited islets of Phournoi, located three miles
south of the coast of Ikaria, boasting natural harbors capable of accommodating various vessels. He further
mentions that at other times, corsairs from Malta and other Christian factions would lie in wait on these islands,
ambushing ships trading between Chios and Rhodes.
The daily routine of these corsair groups is vividly described by the English captive Mr. Roberts, who was
shipwrecked in Ios in 1692 and subsequently captured by pirates, forced to serve as a gunner on their ship.
­According to Roberts, the corsairs would spend the winter in Paros, Antiparos, Melos and Ios until early March.
They would then relocate to Phournoi, where they would lie in wait from early spring to mid-summer, with
lookouts stationed in the mountains overlooking the Samos-Ikaria strait, keeping watch for passing ships. They
would also venture into the southern part of Ikaria, Gaidouronisi and Leipsoi, before moving further south to
posts in Asia Minor, spanning from Cilicia to Cyprus. In autumn, they would return to the Aegean to sell their
plunder and deliver profits to their backers in Livorno, Malta or Marseille (Hacke 1699; Ormerod 1924, 17–8;
Krantonelli 1991, 89–93; Simopoulos 1994, 106).
This cyclic movement of ambush, aligned with the routes of convoys between Alexandria and C
­ onstantinople
or guided by intelligence from captured vessels, was undoubtedly a prevalent method of piracy during this era.

evidence.text:
When Paul I came to the throne in 1796, Malta and Russia had long had
a common enemy. It was the Ottoman Empire, its Muslim Turks, and
its Barbary corsairs. Unlike Malta, a central Mediterranean archipelago
with well-protected, deep-water harbours, Russia had been a largely
landlocked country whose territorial expansion historically had tended
to be across internal frontiers, from Kiev to Muscovy to Kazan. With the
advent of Peter I, however, and especially after his declaration of war
against Turkey and the acquisition of the Black Sea port of Azov in 1696,
Russia began to nurture a naval and maritime policy. This policy was
two-pronged: to the North in the struggle with Sweden for access to the
Baltic; to the South in the long drawn out confrontations with the Turks
in their extensive domains, hemming Russia in from the Mediterranean,
and indeed from the Black Sea.
Paul I's keen interest in Malta and its Catholic, aristocratic order
of chivalry, must be seen in the light of a string of earlier acquaintances,
overtures and schemes of mutual interest between the Czars of
Russia, on one hand, and the Knights of Malta, on the other. Two of
his best known predecessors, Peter I (1672-1725) and Catherine II
(1729-1796), already had set their sights on Malta, its knights and, not
least, its famous fleet. Given the new-found commitment to naval and
maritime undertakings, Petrine Russia now had an ideological as well
as a strategic shared interest with the Mediterranean headquarters of
the anti-Turkish, anti-Muslim crusaders.
From Russia's point of view, this interest was also technical and
. professional, in so far as the successful equipment, organization and
the leadership of its own Russian fleet was concerned. This made
sense, too, in the context of the Western expertise and support which
both Peter and Catherine sought, coveted and to an extent emulated,
The founding editor of Storja in 1978, Henry Frendo has taught in various universities and is the author
of several books; since 1992 he has been Professor of History at the University of Malta.

Islamic law principles and fight with the task of leading forces along
land borders, as a requirement of the Islamic understanding of jihad
and gaza in the seas. For this reason, even when the Ottoman pirates
were fighting in the service of the state or on their own behalf, they
fought a war of faith according to Islamic law. As a result of this, the
Ottoman pirates, who were more often referred to as levend or
voluntary levend in this period, were called harami levend when they
went out of law and were punished for this reason. The main pirates
are the Christians who appeared in the Mediterranean after the 14th
century. Their aim was to capture booty and captives on a large scale.
The Ottoman Empire regulated and helped develop unregulated
Turkish piracy in the Mediterranean beginning at the end of the 14th
century. The famous Turkish pirate of this period, Kemal captain,
burned a Spanish fleet in Andalusian waters with a pirate fleet
prepared by the Ottoman Empire and plundered the city of Malacca.
By making the island of Djerba a base, it became a dangerous enemy
for Christian Europe. Turgut, Piri, and Murad captains tried to turn the
Mediterranean into a Turkish lake by fighting the Spaniards and
Venetians. Meanwhile, İlyas, İshak, Oruç, and Hızır captains, who
began their piracy in North Africa, launched an attack on the Spaniards
and Genoese in the Mediterranean. Suleiman the Magnificent thought
of developing the navy by bringing together the Turkish pirates to turn
the Mediterranean into a Turkish lake. He invited Hızır captain
(Barbaros Hayreddin), who was holding Algeria in his hands, to
Istanbul. He gave him the rank of captain. Barbaros' joining the
Ottoman navy after destroying the Crusader navy in Preveza (1538)
marked the end of Turkish piracy. Uluç Ali captain, who was trained by
him, came to Istanbul by saving his ship even though the Ottoman
navy was defeated in Inebahti (1571); this last pirate was also given
the rank of captain. Until his death (1587), chiefs from Algeria and the

Corsairing was simply another form of aggression,
preying on men, ships, towns, villages, flocks; it meant
eating the food of others in order to remain strong.

bunların tanzim edilmesini ve aynı zamanda Garp Ocakları ile böyle bir durumu bir daha yaşamamak için antlaşma yapmak istediklerini belirtmişlerdir. Bu
olay üzerine 14 Haziran 1725 tarihinde Osmanlı Devleti, İsmail ve Süleyman
isminde iki kapıcıbaşı ile Avusturya adına iki temsilciyi Cezayir’e göndermiş,
lakin Cezayir Dayısı Abdi Paşa, padişahın bu konuda fermanı olmasına rağmen antlaşma yapmayı kabul etmemiştir. Tunus ve Trablusgarp Ocakları ise
Cezayir’in aksine padişahın fermanı doğrultusunda Avusturya ile antlaşma
yapmayı kabul etmişlerdir. Tunus Ocağı ile Avusturya arasında 18 Aralık 1725
tarihinde on üç madden oluşan bir ticaret ve güvenlik antlaşması imzalanmış,
aynı antlaşma yaklaşık iki yıl sonra aynı maddeler üzerinden Nisan 1727 tarihinde Trablusgarp Ocağı ile de akdedilmiştir30.
Yapılan bu antlaşmalara rağmen Garp Ocakları’nın Avusturya ticaret gemilerine saldırıları devam etti. Akdeniz’de bu saldırılardan dolayı büyük ticari
zararlara uğrayan Avusturya mevcut başıboşluktan dolayı Osmanlı yönetimini
sorumlu tutmaya başladı. Elçisi kanalıyla Sultan I. Mahmut’a bir mektup göndererek bundan sonra Garp Ocakları korsanlarının Avusturya tüccar gemilerine
zararı vaki olur ise bu zarar ve ziyanın Osmanlı Devleti tarafından karşılanmasını talep etti31. Lakin Osmanlı Devleti’nin bu dönemde böyle bir sorumluluğu
ve yükümlüğü alması söz konusu değildi.
Garp Ocakları’nın saldırısı sadece Avusturya ticaret gemileri ile sınırlı
değildi. Osmanlı Devleti’nin kapitülasyonlar (1535) ile başlayan ticari ilişkilerini uzun yıllar sıcak tutuğu Fransızları da rahatsız etmekteydi. Zira bu korsanlık faaliyetleri onların da Akdeniz’deki ticari faaliyetlerini sekteye uğratıyordu. 1569 yılında iki ülke arasında bu konuda bir antlaşma dahi imzalanmıştı32.
Lakin XVIII. yüzyılla birlikte Garp Ocakları’nın Fransız ticaret gemilerine olan
korsan saldırıları artmıştı. Örneğin 1742 yılında bu saldırıların birinde Şerabut
isimli kaptanın idaresindeki Fransız ticaret gemisine korsanlar tarafından el
konularak altı yüz kuruş değerindeki malı gasp edilmiştir. Fransız elçisi bu
olaydan dolayı Osmanlı Devleti’ne müracaat edip yardım istemiştir33.

variations, undoubtedly linked to the ancient name of Phournoi, often coexist with variants of the name
“Phournoi”. ­Conversely, from the 18th century onwards, variants of the name “Phournoi” appear to prevail
among ­cartographers.
The Latin transliteration of the ancient Greek name and its variants closely resemble the byzantine term for the
act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras
1982, s.v. κούρσο(ν), κούρσος) and correlate with derivatives of the Italian term corsario, loosely ­translated as
“one who has a license to raid” (letter de course), derived from Medieval Latin term cursarius (­“pirate”, from
Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of
the ancient name of Phournoi and the various terms for loot and corsair in Latin languages and medieval Greek
has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),
­Kleftolimano (harbor of thieves), Fygou (escape), Fylakio (guard-post), Vardia (shift or guard), Tourkolimnionas
(harbor of the Turks), Pano and Kato Maneta (upper and lower Maneta). Many of these names are commonplace along the Aegean coastline and are also encountered on other islands historically associated with piracy.
However, the two bays designated as Pano and Kato Maneta, situated roughly in the middle of the eastern coast
of the main island of Phournoi, warrant further comment.
It is highly probable that these two bays derived their names from the Zakynthian corsair Eustathios ­(Stathis)
Romanos or Manetas, who, between 1678 and 1684, operated as a pirate in the Aegean Sea while based in Melos,
commanding the only Greek privately owned corsair vessel at the time, most probably handed to him after the
death of its former owner, the Maltese corsair Hugues Creviliers (Krantonelli 1994, 289–91). Early records of
his exploits date back to 1683, when the rector of Tenos reported that Stathis Romanos Manetas had seized the
Venetian consul in Paros, extorting a monopoly over the supply of galette to Venetian fleet vessels. In May 1684,
Admiral Gerolamo Cornaro courted him on behalf of the Venetians, granting him a free pass permit (salvocondotto). Manetas subsequently conducted operations across the Aegean, Ionian and southern Adriatic, either
independently or in collaboration with the Venetians and the Knights of Malta (Krantonelli 1991, 300). At
the onset of the 6th Venetian-Turkish war (1684–1699), Morosini appointed him commander of the V

cruiser flotilla, where he actively participated in the sieges of Lefkada and Preveza (Sathas 1869, 312–19; Donos
2007, 74–85, 101). Subsequently, he assisted the Venetian admiral in levying taxes on Aegean islands and aiding
in the sieg

these authors report that Julius Caesar was apprehended near Pharmakoussa. The only exception is Polyaenus,
according to whom the pirates captured their famous victim close to Cape Maleas in the Peloponnese and
­remained outside the walls of Miletus until the ransom was delivered. This reference implicitly suggests that
Pharmakoussa ­belonged to the chora of Miletus.
Plutarch and Polyaenus refer to the pirates who captured Julius Caesar as Cilicians, while the other sources
do not specify their identity. Therefore, it cannot be certain whether the pirates were Cilicians, Milesians or
whether a mixed band − a fairly common occurrence in pirate crews. Perhaps, there was confusion between
the terms Cilicians and pirates (App. Mith. 14.92) or perhaps the pirates presented themselves as coming from
a distant homeland (e.g., Cilicia), to hide their real identity and to protect (nearby) homeland from reprisals, or perhaps the relevant sources, which are all considerably later than the event, wanted to attribute the
incident to some unknown or foreign pirates. Indeed, after the final defeat of Mithridates and the end of the
­Mithridatic wars, cities like Miletus ceased trying to strike a balance between the two conflicting powers (Rome
and ­Mithridates) and sided, willingly or unwillingly, with Rome (see Kleiner 1968, 19; Sarantidis 2020, 55−6;
Cicero (Verr. 2.1.89), likewise, refers to the imposition of taxes “by the Roman people” and the participation of
Miletus in the expulsion of the pirates).
In any event, whether the pirates had Pharmakoussa as their base or were operating outside of it, or
whether they happened to locate themselves in the vicinity only once, it is difficult to accept the idea that they
went ­unnoticed by a passing ship or by guard troops, given the presence of defensive forts and watchtowers
throughout the Milesian seaboard territories, including those on Pharmakoussa itself (for the supervision of
these islands, see Sarantidis 2020, 203–23, figs. 112–21). Moreover, both the undisturbed visit of a large group of
men anchored in an island cove for thirty-eight days, and the fact that Julius Caesar himself, after he redeemed
himself and assembled a fleet, returned to the island to find the pirates still situated at the same place, would
seem to indicate that the pirates in question were able to reside on these islands (or, at least, on Pharmakoussa)
and conduct their activities unhindered during this period.
However, pirate activity in this islandscape was not limited to antiquity; in fact, pirates continued to operate
there in modern times. The Englishman Anthony Roberts, a pirate who was himself taken hostage by pirates in
1692, describes the seasonal but systematic use of the region by pirates, stating that after wintering on islands,
such as Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Melos, pirates would sail to Phournoi in early March: “And then they go for the
Furnoes [Phournoi], and lie there under the high land hid, having a watch on the hill with a little flag, whereby
they make a signal, if they see any sail; they flip out, and lie athwart the boak of Samos, and take their prize;
they lie in the same nature under Necaria [Ikaria], and Gadronise [Gaidouronisi], and Leppiso [Leipsoi] in
the spring and forepart of the summer” (Hacke 1699, 8; see also Koutsouflakis, this volume; Koutzakiotis, this
volume). It should be noted that Gaidouronisi is an earlier name for Agathonisi, which continued to be used as
a pirate site in the following century (see Krantonelli 1998, 110, 179).
